title: MITCHELL-RILEY SYNDROME
alt_titles: DIABETES, NEONATAL, WITH PANCREATIC HYPOPLASIA, INTESTINAL ATRESIA, AND GALLBLADDER APLASIA OR HYPOPLASIA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Mitchell-Riley syndrome (MTCHRS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RFX6 gene on chromosome 6q21-q22.

checks.claim: Mitchell-Riley syndrome (MTCHRS) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the RFX6 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Biallelic mutations in RFX6 (regulatory factor X, 6) cause neonatal diabetes mellitus in association with intestinal atresias, and hepatobiliary abnormalities. This condition has been designated as Mitchell–Riley syndrome.
checks.explanation: Biallelic mutations cause the disorder. The table lists both homozygous and compound heterozygous cases.

checks.claim: The RFX6 gene is located on chromosome 6q21-q22.
checks.explanation: the audit returned no verdict for this claim

paragraphs.text: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, duodenal and/or jejunal atresia or intestinal malrotation, and gallbladder aplasia or hypoplasia (Mitchell et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2010). Affected infants often have low birth weight, intrahepatic cholestasis, and malabsorption that does not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement, and many die within the first year of life (Mitchell et al., 2004; Smith et al., 2010; Sansbury et al., 2015). Sansbury et al. (2015) reported patients with the typical intestinal atresias whose diabetes did not begin until childhood.

checks.claim: Mitchell-Riley syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: This combination of multiple congenital abnormalities has not been previously described and probably represents a new autosomal recessive syndrome
checks.explanation: Paper proposes autosomal recessive inheritance as probable; the draft states it as established fact.

checks.claim: The main features of Mitchell-Riley syndrome are neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, duodenal and/or jejunal atresia or intestinal malrotation, and gallbladder aplasia or hypoplasia.

checks.explanation: Core features match, but intestinal malrotation is not mentioned in the abstract.

checks.evidence_quote: All cases had evidence of liver involvement with intrahepatic cholestasis in 7/8 cases and ascites in a further case.

checks.evidence_quote: Here we report two individuals born to double first cousins in whom intestinal atresias consistent with a diagnosis of Mitchell-Riley syndrome were diagnosed at birth, but in whom diabetes did not present until the ages of 3 and 6 years.

paragraphs.text: Martínez-Frías et al. (1992) described 2 sibs, born to consanguineous parents, with low birth weight, tracheoesophageal fistula, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias. They suggested this was a previously unreported autosomal recessive syndrome. A search of the Spanish Collaborative Study of Congenital Malformations (ECEMC) found 3 other unrelated infants with intestinal atresias, hypospadias, and low birth weight, who might represent a milder form of the same syndrome. Related reports followed. Annerén et al. (1998) reported a lethal autosomal recessive syndrome of intrauterine growth retardation, intra- and extrahepatic biliary atresia, and esophageal and duodenal atresia. Gentile and Fiorente (1999) reported esophageal, duodenal, rectoanal, and biliary atresia, intestinal malrotation, malformed/hypoplastic pancreas, and hypospadias. Galán-Gómez et al. (2007) described a patient born to consanguineous parents with low birth weight, duodenal atresia, extrahepatic biliary atresia, hypoplastic pancreas, and intestinal malrotation, and considered her a further example of the Martínez-Frías syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Chappell et al. (2008) proposed that cases with overlapping features, including those described by Martínez-Frías, might be variants of the same syndrome. Martinovici et al. (2010) diagnosed Martínez-Frías syndrome in a newborn with intestinal atresia, gallbladder aplasia, and diabetes mellitus. Smith et al. (2010), however, noted that the original Martínez-Frías patients had esophageal atresia and hypospadias and did not have diabetes. They also found no RFX6 mutation in the parents of one case of Martínez-Frías syndrome. On this basis, they concluded that their RFX6-mutated cases were distinct from Martínez-Frías syndrome. They proposed the name Mitchell-Riley syndrome, after the 2 clinicians who first described the condition.

paragraphs.text: Mitchell et al. (2004) described 5 infants with neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, jejunal atresia, duodenal atresia, and gallbladder aplasia or hypoplasia. The infants came from 2 sib pairs in 2 families plus 1 isolated case, and one sib pair was born to consanguineous parents. One patient had a milder form and was surviving without insulin. The other 4 children died in the first year of life despite aggressive medical management. Pancreatic immunohistochemistry in 3 infants showed a few scattered chromogranin A-positive cell clusters but no insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin. Exocrine histology varied. Mitchell et al. (2004) concluded that this combination probably represented a new autosomal recessive syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Chappell et al. (2008) reported a patient, born to consanguineous parents, with neonatal diabetes, intestinal atresias, and gallbladder agenesis. This was the first such case with neonatal diabetes but no demonstrable structural abnormality of the pancreas. In a later review, Sansbury et al. (2015) identified this patient as a Pakistani girl born at 35 weeks' gestation weighing 1,700 g. She had onset of diabetes on day 8, duodenal atresia, malrotation, undetectable fecal elastase, intrahepatic cholestasis, and an anteriorly placed anus, and was alive at 1 year 9 months.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) described patients with neonatal diabetes and small bowel obstruction due to bowel atresia. Their pancreata were somewhat small, but the patients were not deficient in exocrine pancreatic enzymes. Autopsies of 2 cases showed normal-appearing exocrine pancreata containing clusters of chromogranin A-positive cells, with no cells staining for insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin. The syndrome also included a hypoplastic gallbladder and intractable diarrhea that did not respond to pancreatic enzyme replacement.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) reported 2 Turkish double first cousins with intestinal atresias at birth whose diabetes did not present until ages 3 and 6 years. There was no history of parental consanguinity, but the mothers of the 2 patients were sisters and the fathers were brothers. The first patient was a girl born at 32 weeks' gestation weighing 1.65 kg, with duodenal atresia, a jejunal web, and Meckel diverticulum. Hyperglycemia (10.6 mmol/l) was noted at age 2 years, and she presented with diabetic ketoacidosis at age 3 years. At that time, insulin was less than 2 microIU/ml, C-peptide was 0.023 ng/ml, and anti-GAD, IAA, and ICA antibodies were negative. She had repeated gastrointestinal bleeding, and a small intestinal resection at age 5 years showed patches of gastric heterotopia. She also had an absent gallbladder, with an otherwise normal biliary tract and normal liver function. Her identical twin had duodenal atresia and died at 1 month of age from complications of prematurity and surgery.

paragraphs.text: The second patient described by Sansbury et al. (2015) was a boy born at 34 weeks' gestation weighing 1.70 kg, with duodenal atresia and midgut malrotation. He was diagnosed with diabetes at age 6 years, when hyperglycemia (16.0 mmol/l) was found. Asymptomatic fasting hyperglycemia had been noted 1 year earlier. Autoantibodies were negative, and he required about 0.7 units/kg of insulin per day. He also had chronic iron deficiency anemia of unknown cause. No structural hepatobiliary abnormality was found, and his liver function was normal. Sansbury et al. (2015) compared these 2 patients with 8 previously reported molecularly confirmed cases. All 8 earlier cases had duodenal atresia, and 7 of 8 had gallbladder agenesis. All had liver involvement, with intrahepatic cholestasis in 7 and ascites in 1, and 5 had died within the first year of life. Apart from the later onset of diabetes, the 2 new patients differed from earlier cases in having no liver pathology, and they survived longer.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) studied patients with this syndrome, including those reported by Mitchell et al. (2004), Chappell et al. (2008), and Martinovici et al. (2010). They used 2 independent approaches. First, they captured and deep-sequenced the exons in the shared homozygous regions in 1 proband. This identified 30 novel variants, of which the only nonsynonymous change was a homozygous ser217-to-pro (S217P) mutation in the RFX6 gene. Second, direct sequencing of RFX6 found missense, splice site, or frameshift mutations in 5 of 6 probands. Four probands were homozygous for these mutations and 1 was compound heterozygous, and all mutations were inherited from carrier parents. In 1 proband homozygous for a splice site mutation, RT-PCR of autopsy pancreas detected no properly spliced RFX6 transcript. In an electrophoretic mobility shift assay, the R181Q mutation completely abolished DNA binding, whereas the S217P mutation reduced it only modestly. No RFX6 mutation was found in 1 proband, whose DNA was unavailable and who was considered most likely a phenocopy. Smith et al. (2010) also found no RFX6 mutations in a case of Martínez-Frías syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Sansbury et al. (2015) used targeted next-generation sequencing of 29 monogenic diabetes genes in the Turkish double first cousins with childhood-onset diabetes. Both patients were compound heterozygous for 2 nonsense mutations in the RFX6 gene, R726X and R866X, located in exons 17 and 18. The fathers carried the R726X mutation and the mothers carried the R866X mutation, and both mutations had been inherited from the grandmothers. Several heterozygous relatives had adult-onset diabetes. However, C-peptide and HbA1c measurements did not support heterozygosity for either mutation as a risk factor for diabetes.

paragraphs.text: Smith et al. (2010) generated Rfx6-null mice by replacing the first 5 exons, which include the DNA-binding domain, with an eGFP-cre cassette. Homozygous mutant mice were born at the expected mendelian ratio. They fed poorly, had gross bowel distension due to small bowel obstruction, and died within 2 days of birth. Some had a reduced pancreas size. Mutant pancreata still contained many chromogranin A-positive and synaptophysin-positive endocrine cells, but none expressed insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, or ghrelin. Pancreatic polypeptide-expressing cells were increased in number. Neurog3 expression was unaffected, whereas expression of Arx, Irx2, Pax6, Mafa, Neurod1, and Pdx1 was reduced. Smith et al. (2010) concluded that Rfx6 acts downstream of Neurog3 to direct islet cell differentiation.

checks.evidence_quote: The exon 18 mutation, c.2596C>T (R866X) is predicted to escape nonsense-mediated decay because it lies within 50 nucleotides of the last exon–exon boundary of the gene.

checks.claim: The RFX6 R866X mutation was predicted to escape nonsense-mediated decay and to produce a truncated protein that keeps the DNA-binding domain.
checks.evidence_quote: A partially truncated version of the wild-type protein, which comprises 928 amino acids, is therefore predicted to be produced, possibly with some function given the full preservation of the DNA-binding domain.
